summary: A license to remotely access prewritten software is a taxable sale of tangible personal property when the purchaser uses it in New York, sourced to where the purchaser uses or directs use of the software.

citations.title: TSB-A-08(62)S (Adobe Systems, November 24, 2008)
citations.quote: We conclude that the product sold by Petitioner is prewritten computer software that is subject to State and local sales taxes when accessed by a customer located in New York.

citations.title: TB-ST-128 (issued August 5, 2014)
citations.quote: Accordingly, the sale to a purchaser in New York of a license to remotely access software is subject to state and local sales tax.

citations.title: TB-ST-128 (issued August 5, 2014)
citations.quote: The situs of the sale for purposes of determining the proper local tax rate and jurisdiction is the location from which the purchaser uses or directs the use of the software

citations.title: NY Tax Law §1210(a)(1)
citations.quote: shall be identical, except as to rate and except as otherwise provided

citations.title: NY Tax Law §1109 (MCTD additional tax)
citations.quote: which shall be identical to the taxes imposed by sections eleven hundred five and eleven hundred ten of this article

notes: Prewritten software has been taxable since 1991-09-01 (TSB-M-93(3)S), but the earliest official statement read here that remote access counts is TSB-A-08(62)S of 2008-11-24 (an advisory opinion, binding only on its petitioner, but stating the Department's position, later adopted in TB-ST-128). Whether the Department applied it to remote access between 1991 and 2008 is unverified. Multi-state users: tax only the portion of the receipt attributable to users in New York (TB-ST-128). TB-ST-128 itself states 'state and local', so locals follow. Local taxes (Tax Law §1210) and the MCTD 0.375% (Tax Law §1109) follow the state base and exemptions for this code; the local opt-outs NY allows (clothing, residential energy, solar) and the NYC-only services list in Pub 750 do not touch it.

notes: Date is Pub 862's edition (4/01), day unknown, so 2001-04-01 is the first of that month; the treatment is older but earlier dates are unverified. On an exempt capital improvement the contractor pays tax on its materials and builds it into the price; no tax is charged to the customer (TB-ST-104). Installing items that stay tangible personal property (freestanding appliances, canvas awnings) is a taxable installation service (TB-ST-129). Some work is classified case by case; Pub 862 lists many items. The code fixes 'sold to the owner', so the tenant leasehold rule does not arise. The §1105(c)(3)(iii) quote is the capital-improvement exclusion read from the statute page; WebFetch located it under (c)(3)(iii), consistent with TB-ST-740's citation. Local taxes (Tax Law §1210) and the MCTD 0.375% (Tax Law §1109) follow the state base and exemptions for this code; the local opt-outs NY allows (clothing, residential energy, solar) and the NYC-only services list in Pub 750 do not touch it.
